name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Respiratory substrates, ATP, and plant gas exchange

questiontext.text:
Assess the following five statements regarding cellular respiration and gaseous exchange in plants:

Statement I: Usually carbohydrates are oxidised to release energy, though proteins, fats, and organic acids can also serve as respiratory substrates in some plants under certain conditions.

Statement II: Energy released by oxidation in respiration cannot be used directly and is instead trapped in \(\text{ATP}\), which acts as the energy currency of the cell.

Statement III: Plants possess specialised respiratory organs analogous to animal lungs for rapid bulk transport of \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\).

Statement IV: Stomata and lenticels allow gaseous exchange in plants by diffusion.

Statement V: Loose packing of parenchyma cells in leaves, stems, and roots provides an interconnected network of air spaces.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cellular respiration oxidises organic substrates in controlled steps to synthesise \(\text{ATP}\), while plants accomplish gaseous exchange locally by diffusion without specialised respiratory organs.

Step 2: Evaluation of Substrates and ATP
Carbohydrates are the usual respiratory substrates, although proteins, fats, and organic acids can also be oxidised in some plants under specific conditions. The energy liberated during oxidation is not usable directly by cellular processes; instead, it is conserved as \(\text{ATP}\), the energy currency of the cell.

Step 3: Evaluation of Plant Gas-Exchange Systems
Plants do not possess specialised respiratory organs for bulk gas transport; each plant part meets its own gas-exchange needs locally. Stomata and lenticels permit diffusion of gases, and loosely packed parenchyma cells in leaves, stems, and roots form an interconnected network of air spaces that keeps most living cells close to air.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions concerning alternative respiratory substrates, \(\text{ATP}\) as energy currency, diffusion through stomata and lenticels, and interconnected air spaces in parenchyma are correct, whereas the proposition claiming plants have specialised respiratory organs for bulk gas transport is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I, II, III, and IV only
Statements I, II, IV, and V only
Statements II, III, IV, and V only
Statements I, III, IV, and V only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Reactions and energetics of glycolysis and fermentation

questiontext.text:
Assess the following five statements regarding glycolysis and fermentation:

Statement I: Glycolysis (the EMP pathway) occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and is present in all living organisms.

Statement II: In plants, sucrose is cleaved into glucose and fructose by the enzyme hexokinase.

Statement III: \(\text{ATP}\) is utilised at two steps in glycolysis: conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate and conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

Statement IV: \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is formed during the conversion of \(\text{PGAL}\) to \(\text{BPGA}\), and \(\text{ATP}\) is directly synthesised during the conversions of \(\text{BPGA}\) to \(\text{PGA}\) and \(\text{PEP}\) to pyruvic acid.

Statement V: In both lactic acid and alcoholic fermentation, less than 7 per cent of the energy in glucose is released, yielding a net gain of 2 \(\text{ATP}\) molecules per glucose.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glycolysis is the universal cytosolic pathway of partial glucose oxidation, and fermentation regenerates \(\text{NAD}^+\) anaerobically with a net yield of 2 \(\text{ATP}\) per glucose.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sucrose Cleavage and Glycolytic Steps
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms. In plants, sucrose is hydrolysed into glucose and fructose by the enzyme invertase—not hexokinase (which instead phosphorylates glucose and fructose into glucose-6-phosphate). Two \(\text{ATP}\) molecules are consumed during glucose-to-glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate-to-fructose-1,6-bisphosphate conversions. \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is generated when \(\text{PGAL}\) is converted to \(\text{BPGA}\), and \(\text{ATP}\) is directly synthesised at \(\text{BPGA} \rightarrow \text{PGA}\) and \(\text{PEP} \rightarrow \text{pyruvic acid}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Fermentation Energetics
During lactic acid and alcoholic fermentation, less than 7 per cent of the energy in glucose is released, and the net \(\text{ATP}\) gain remains 2 \(\text{ATP}\) per molecule of glucose.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding the cytosolic EMP pathway, the two \(\text{ATP}\)-consuming steps, \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{ATP}\) synthesis steps, and the energetics of fermentation are correct, whereas the proposition attributing sucrose cleavage to hexokinase instead of invertase is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I, II, III, and IV only
Statements I, II, IV, and V only
Statements II, III, IV, and V only
Statements I, III, IV, and V only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Mitochondrial matrix oxidation of pyruvate and TCA cycle

questiontext.text:
Assess the following five statements regarding aerobic oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix:

Statement I: Pyruvate formed in the cytosol is transported into the mitochondrial matrix, where it undergoes oxidative decarboxylation.

Statement II: Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), \(\text{NAD}^+\), and Coenzyme A to convert pyruvic acid into acetyl \(\text{CoA}\), \(\text{CO}_2\), and \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\).

Statement III: Citrate synthase catalyses the condensation of the acetyl group with oxaloacetic acid (\(\text{OAA}\)) and water to yield citric acid.

Statement IV: Following isomerisation of citrate to isocitrate, three successive decarboxylation steps occur before succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\) is formed.

Statement V: In one turn of the citric acid cycle, \(\text{NAD}^+\) is reduced at three points, \(\text{FAD}^+\) is reduced at one point, and one \(\text{GTP}\) molecule is synthesised by substrate-level phosphorylation.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aerobic oxidation of pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix comprises the link reaction (pyruvate dehydrogenase) and the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs') cycle.

Step 2: Evaluation of Link Reaction and Cycle Initiation
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix and undergoes oxidative decarboxylation catalysed by pyruvate dehydrogenase in the presence of \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), \(\text{NAD}^+\), and \(\text{CoA}\) to form acetyl \(\text{CoA}\), \(\text{CO}_2\), and \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\). Acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) then condenses with oxaloacetic acid and water via citrate synthase to form citric acid.

Step 3: Evaluation of Decarboxylations and Cycle Outputs
After citrate is isomerised to isocitrate, only two successive decarboxylation steps—not three—occur to form \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\). In each turn of the cycle, \(\text{NAD}^+\) is reduced at three points, \(\text{FAD}^+\) is reduced at one point, and one \(\text{GTP}\) is formed by substrate-level phosphorylation during succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\) conversion to succinic acid.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding mitochondrial pyruvate transport, pyruvate dehydrogenase cofactors, citrate synthase initiation, and the count of \(\text{NADH}\), \(\text{FADH}_2\), and \(\text{GTP}\) per turn are correct, whereas the proposition claiming three successive decarboxylations before succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\) formation is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I, II, III, and V only
Statements I, II, III, and IV only
Statements I, III, IV, and V only
Statements II, III, IV, and V only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - ETS complexes, ATP synthase, and balance sheet assumptions

questiontext.text:
Assess the following five statements regarding the Electron Transport System (ETS), oxidative phosphorylation, and the respiratory balance sheet:

Statement I: Both Complex I (\(\text{NADH}\) dehydrogenase) and Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) transfer electrons to ubiquinone within the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Statement II: Cytochrome \(c\) is a small mobile carrier protein attached to the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane that transfers electrons between Complex III and Complex IV.

Statement III: Complex IV (cytochrome \(c\) oxidase) contains cytochromes \(a\) and \(a_3\) along with two copper centres, and \(\text{O}_2\) acts as the final hydrogen acceptor.

Statement IV: For each \(\text{ATP}\) produced by Complex V (\(\text{ATP}\) synthase), \(2\text{H}^+\) passes through the \(\text{F}_0\) channel from the intermembrane space to the matrix.

Statement V: The theoretical net gain of 38 \(\text{ATP}\) molecules per glucose assumes that TCA cycle intermediates are continuously withdrawn to synthesise amino acids and fatty acids.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The inner mitochondrial membrane houses Complexes I–IV of the ETS and Complex V (\(\text{ATP}\) synthase), coupling redox-driven proton translocation to \(\text{ATP}\) synthesis, while the 38 \(\text{ATP}\) balance sheet rests on strict idealised assumptions.

Step 2: Evaluation of ETS Carriers and ATP Synthase
Ubiquinone receives electrons from both Complex I (\(\text{NADH}\) dehydrogenase) and Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase via \(\text{FADH}_2\)). Reduced ubiquinone transfers electrons to Complex III (cytochrome \(bc_1\)), and cytochrome \(c\)—a mobile carrier on the outer surface of the inner membrane—shuttles electrons from Complex III to Complex IV. Complex IV contains cytochromes \(a\), \(a_3\), and two copper centres, passing electrons to \(\text{O}_2\) as the final hydrogen acceptor. At Complex V, \(2\text{H}^+\) moves through \(\text{F}_0\) from the intermembrane space to the matrix per \(\text{ATP}\) formed at \(\text{F}_1\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Balance Sheet Assumptions
The theoretical calculation of 38 \(\text{ATP}\) per glucose specifically assumes that none of the intermediates in the pathway are utilised to synthesise any other compound. Claiming that it assumes continuous withdrawal of intermediates for amino acid and fatty acid synthesis is therefore incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions detailing ubiquinone electron entry from Complexes I and II, cytochrome \(c\) shuttling between Complexes III and IV, Complex IV composition with \(\text{O}_2\) as final acceptor, and \(2\text{H}^+\) flow per \(\text{ATP}\) through \(\text{F}_0\) are correct, whereas the proposition claiming the 38 \(\text{ATP}\) calculation assumes intermediate withdrawal is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I, II, III, and V only
Statements I, II, IV, and V only
Statements I, II, III, and IV only
Statements II, III, IV, and V only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Amphibolic pathway and respiratory quotient values

questiontext.text:
Assess the following five statements regarding the amphibolic pathway and respiratory quotient (\(\text{RQ}\)):

Statement I: When fats are respired, fatty acids are converted to \(\text{PGAL}\) and glycerol is degraded to acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) before entering the respiratory pathway.

Statement II: Proteins are degraded by proteases into amino acids, which after deamination enter the respiratory pathway at some stage within the Krebs' cycle or as pyruvate or acetyl \(\text{CoA}\).

Statement III: Because intermediates such as acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) can be withdrawn from the respiratory pathway for fatty acid synthesis, the respiratory pathway is amphibolic rather than purely catabolic.

Statement IV: The respiratory quotient (\(\text{RQ}\)) is \(1.0\) for complete oxidation of glucose, \(0.7\) for tripalmitin, and about \(0.9\) for proteins.

Statement V: In living organisms, respiratory substrates are often more than one, and pure proteins or fats are never used as sole respiratory substrates.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The respiratory pathway integrates carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism for both energy release (catabolism) and biosynthesis (anabolism), and the \(\text{RQ}\) depends on the substrate oxidised.

Step 2: Evaluation of Fat and Protein Entry Points
When fats are broken down, fatty acids are degraded to acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) and glycerol is converted to 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (\(\text{PGAL}\))—reversing these two entry points is incorrect. For proteins, proteases yield amino acids which, after deamination, enter the Krebs' cycle or enter as pyruvate or acetyl \(\text{CoA}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Amphibolic Role and RQ Values
Because intermediates like acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) are also withdrawn for biosynthesis (such as fatty acid synthesis), the pathway is amphibolic. The \(\text{RQ} = \frac{\text{volume of } \text{CO}_2 \text{ evolved}}{\text{volume of } \text{O}_2 \text{ consumed}}\) equals \(1.0\) for glucose, \(0.7\) for tripalmitin (\(\frac{102}{145}\)), and about \(0.9\) for proteins. In living organisms, multiple substrates are respired together, and pure proteins or fats are never used alone.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding amino acid entry points, the amphibolic nature of respiration, the \(\text{RQ}\) values for glucose, tripalmitin, and proteins, and mixed substrate utilisation in vivo are correct, whereas the proposition reversing the entry points of fatty acids and glycerol is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I, II, III, and IV only
Statements II, III, IV, and V only
Statements I, III, IV, and V only
Statements I, II, IV, and V only
